title: Late-night homicide solved on call-tower + deleted SMS
description: Accused Ramesh was suspected in the murder of deceased Sunil after a property dispute. Deceased was last seen leaving his shop at 22:10. Accused denied being at the scene.

artifacts.note: Two calls to the deceased at 22:04 and 22:31 contradicted the accused's alibi.

Established the accused-deceased relationship.
Bulk gallery pull produced nothing of evidentiary value; 40 minutes of acquisition wasted.
No relevant history.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; convicted at trial.
lessons: In homicide, movement + call graph around the time of death carry the case.
Bulk media is usually dead weight unless scene or weapon photographs are alleged.

title: Homicide where gallery media was the decisive artifact

Trashed-media recovery outperformed live gallery listing.

title: Kidnapping resolved on ransom-call trail and movement history

title: Data-theft insider identified from app usage and cloud accounts

Account addition events are a strong exfiltration signal.

title: Stalking and threat case built entirely from messaging threads

title: Missing person located from last-known movement and travel search

title: Conspiracy case requiring all-source collection

Reconnaissance is visible as repeat location visits plus geotagged media of the same place.

title: Homicide where the notification log preserved deleted message content
description: Accused Prakash was suspected in the death of deceased Manoj. The accused wiped the messaging application before seizure.

Nothing relevant.

Application data-clear timestamps are themselves evidence.

title: Blackmail case resolved from Wi-Fi and Bluetooth association history
description: Complainant Ishita reported blackmail by an unknown person who demonstrated physical proximity. Suspect Ajay was identified later.

Burner-number cases still leave device-association traces.

title: Cheating case where screen-time and usage statistics disproved a defence

outcome: Defence rejected; convicted.

Always collect the cheap behavioural artifacts — they defeat alibi defences.

title: Custodial abduction where calendar and travel artifacts carried the case
description: Complainant Sneha reported that accused Manish removed their child from lawful custody and left the state.

artifacts.note: A travel entry created before the removal established premeditation.
Ticket and accommodation searches identified the destination.
Route reconstruction supported interception.
Booking confirmations tied to a specific account.
Contact with a relative at the destination.
Nothing additional recovered.

outcome: Child recovered; accused arrested.
lessons: Calendar entries are routinely deprioritised but prove premeditation in planned-removal cases.
Travel-intent artifacts (calendar, browser, accounts) cluster together and should be planned as a group.

title: Contract killing where the money trail replaced an absent call graph
description: FIR 214/2024 u/s 103 and 61 BNS, PS Hadapsar. Accused Dhiraj was suspected of engaging an assailant to kill deceased Ashok over a land dispute. The accused's handset showed no contact whatsoever with the person who attacked the deceased, and the accused relied on that absence.

artifacts.note: Two UPI transfers of Rs 25,000 on 4 and 11 February to a VPA later resolved to the assailant, both annotated 'labour advance'.
Bank debit alerts preserved the payee VPA and the transaction reference after the payment application itself had been uninstalled.
Uninstall timestamp of the payment application, two days after the offence, evidenced an attempt to remove the trail.
Handset remained at the accused's residence through the offence window, consistent with engagement of a third party rather than presence.
Read in full. All coordination ran on a separate prepaid handset never recovered; the seized handset's call log held no contact with the assailant at all.
The assailant was never saved in the address book; the contact list contributed nothing.
Family photographs only; nothing of evidentiary value.
Device unrooted; msgstore.db.crypt15 present but the key could not be extracted, so the thread was never read either way.

outcome: Charge-sheeted for murder and criminal conspiracy; the assailant was traced from the payee VPA and later arrested.
lessons: A contract killing deliberately leaves no contact between the accused and the scene — follow the money instead of the call graph.
Bank debit SMS survives the uninstall of the payment application and preserves the payee identifier when the app's own history is gone.
Record an empty call log as a genuine 'none': it was read, and its emptiness is what pointed the investigation at the financial artifacts.

title: Fake-invoice racket where the photo gallery was the document repository
description: FIR 61/2024 u/s 318(4) and 336 BNS, PS Bhiwandi. Accused Jitendra and co-accused Salman were alleged to have issued invoices from three non-existent firms to enable fraudulent input-tax claims. Complainant was the State Tax Officer.

artifacts.note: 214 photographs of forged invoices, three rubber stamps and signed blank letterheads of the shell firms, stored in the WhatsApp Images folder.
Exported chat text in Download, together with the Sent media folder, showed the invoices being circulated to eleven buyers on demand.
Forty further invoice images recovered from the .trashed- directory in shared storage.
UPI receipts of a two per cent commission from six of those buyers.
Read in full. The tax portal was only ever accessed from a desktop; the handset browser history held nothing relevant.
Movement history was read and was irrelevant to a documentary offence.
Foreground statistics added nothing to the case.
Installed, but the handset was unrooted and cache4.db could not be read.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; input-tax credit of Rs 4.1 crore reversed and two receivers arrested.
lessons: Documentary fraud lives in the photo gallery — the accused photographs paper rather than storing files, so media is a high-value artifact in fraud, not a low one.
WhatsApp Media and Sent folders in shared storage are readable without root even when the message database is not.

title: Remote-access banking fraud proved from install time and foreground usage
description: FIR 305/2024 u/s 319(2) and 318(4) BNS r/w 66D IT Act, PS Malleswaram. Complainant Lakshmi lost Rs 6.8 lakh across four debits after a caller posing as bank support persuaded her to install a screen-sharing application. Her own handset was examined; no suspect was identified at intake.

artifacts.note: A screen-sharing application installed eleven minutes before the first debit and never used again; install source was a link, not the store.
Foreground timeline placed the screen-sharing application in the foreground across all four debits, establishing the mechanism.
The four OTP messages had been deleted from the handset during the session; all four were carved from the SMS freelist, showing the complainant never forwarded them.
Surviving debit alerts fixed the amounts and timeline.
The single inbound call from a spoofed number, spanning the whole session.
Payment-application records identified the three beneficiary accounts.
Read in full and empty of anything relevant — the fraud used a phone call and a direct download link, so nothing was ever browsed.
The caller was never saved; the address book contributed nothing.
Database was readable and was searched; the complainant had no contact with the fraudster on it. Forty minutes of Tier-2 effort for nothing.

outcome: Beneficiary accounts frozen within the golden hour; Rs 4.2 lakh recovered; investigation into the mule network continuing.
lessons: Fraud committed through a remote-access session leaves its evidence in app install time and foreground usage, not in any message thread.
Always carve deleted SMS on a victim handset before concluding the OTPs were shared — recovering them is what distinguishes negligence from deception.

title: Narcotics supply proved by proof-of-quantity photographs when chats were empty
description: FIR 47/2024 u/s 8(c) r/w 20(b)(ii)(B) NDPS Act, PS Anjuna. Accused Sunny was found in possession of a commercial quantity of ganja. The handset was rooted at the laboratory, so both chat databases were fully readable.

artifacts.note: Nineteen photographs of weighed packets on a kitchen scale, sent as proof-of-quantity to buyers; EXIF placed them at the accused's premises.
Sixteen of those photographs had been deleted and were recovered from the thumbnail cache at full evidential quality.
Contact with two buyers within four minutes of each image being sent.
Two repeat handover points on the coastal road, five visits each.
Both repeat buyers were saved with nicknames.
Root-recovered msgstore.db was fully readable and was read in full. Disappearing messages had been enabled for seven months; the surviving thread held only greetings. Readable and genuinely empty.
cache4.db read successfully; only public channel subscriptions, no case-related conversation of any kind.
Payment applications and bank SMS were read; the trade was entirely in cash and left no digital payment trace whatsoever.

outcome: Charge-sheeted under NDPS; two buyers arraigned on the photograph trail.
lessons: Disappearing-message settings leave a readable database that is genuinely empty — that is a 'none', not an access failure, and it should shift effort onto media rather than onto rooting the next handset.
Proof-of-quantity photographs are a fixed habit in retail narcotics supply; carve the thumbnail cache even when the live gallery looks clean.
A cash-only network produces a real financial 'none'; recording it stops the next plan promising a payment trail that will not exist.

title: Dark-net narcotics vendor: browser, accounts and crypto inverted the usual profile
description: FIR 12/2025 u/s 8(c) r/w 22(c) NDPS Act, PS Cyber Crime Bengaluru. Accused Rachit was alleged to have sourced psychotropic tablets from an overseas marketplace and redistributed them by courier to rented postal addresses across four states.

artifacts.note: Onion-mirror history plus courier tracking pages for eleven consignments, each matching a seized parcel.
Three throwaway mail accounts used for marketplace registration and vendor feedback, all still signed in.
USDT wallet addresses in the clipboard buffer and a crypto-exchange application's full transaction list.
A sideloaded onion browser and a non-custodial wallet, both installed outside the store.
Vendor-support channel confirming order numbers.
Read in full. Courier delivery OTPs only; no coded traffic and no counterparty messaging.
Read in full and empty of counterparty contact — this network never used voice at any point.
Movement history was complete and showed the accused never went near any of the eleven delivery addresses. Deliberate, and evidentially empty.
Installed and registered, but the handset was unrooted and the crypt15 database could not be decrypted.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; two overseas vendor accounts referred through the MLAT channel.
lessons: Dark-net narcotics inverts the usual NDPS profile: browser, accounts and crypto traces outrank call logs and GPS entirely.
A courier-based supply chain deliberately breaks the link between the handset's location and the delivery address — absence of GPS overlap is a finding, not an exculpatory fact.

title: Online radicalisation case carried by browser and hidden media alone
description: RC 04/2024 u/s 13 and 38 UAPA. Accused Shahnawaz was alleged to have consumed and stored proscribed-organisation propaganda and to have been in contact with a handler. No physical plot was alleged and no target was identified.

artifacts.note: Sustained access to a proscribed organisation's publication archive over fourteen months, with download timestamps for thirty-one issues.
Nine hundred propaganda images and three instructional videos in a .nomedia directory, invisible to the gallery but found on a filesystem walk.
Fragments of four cleared PDFs carved from the browser cache partition.
Two pseudonymous accounts used for forum registration.
A secure-messaging application installed eleven months earlier and its data cleared three days before seizure.
Application data had been cleared before seizure; nothing survived even after the handset was rooted. Not read, so not a yield.
Read in full; family and workplace calls only, nothing of interest.
Bank SMS and payment applications read; no transfers in or out. The accused was self-funded and there was no funding trail to find.
Complete movement history read; home, workplace and mosque only. No reconnaissance of any kind, because there was no physical plot.
Address book was family and colleagues; handler contact was entirely in-application and never saved.

outcome: Charge-sheeted under Sections 13 and 38 UAPA on possession and association.
lessons: Not every UAPA case has a recce and a funding trail — an online radicalisation case can be entirely browser and media, with location, financial and contact artifacts genuinely empty.
A .nomedia directory hides content from the gallery but not from a filesystem walk; never accept the gallery listing as the media inventory.
A cleared application is inaccessible, not empty — grading it 'none' would teach the tool to stop asking for chat databases in terror cases.

title: Terror-funding collector where money and contacts carried the case and media was empty
description: RC 09/2024 u/s 17 and 40 UAPA. Accused Iqbal was alleged to have collected small contributions from twenty-six persons under a welfare pretext and aggregated them for onward transfer. He never approached any target and held no propaganda.

artifacts.note: Layered UPI credits from twenty-six contributors, aggregated within forty-eight hours and forwarded to two accounts through a hawala intermediary.
Bank alerts preserved the entire transfer chain after the payment application's own history had been cleared.
Twenty-two of the twenty-six payer names in the alerts matched saved contacts, identifying the contributor network.
Collection reminders preserved in an exported chat text file in Download.
Cleared payment-application notification records recovered from notification history.
Two payment identities on one handset.
Full gallery pull ran fifty-five minutes and produced nothing — no propaganda, no reconnaissance photographs, no documents.
Movement history read in full; residence, shop and bank only. A funding node has no operational movement to find.
Read in full; no relevant history.
Installed; handset unrooted and cache4.db unreadable at the time of examination.

outcome: Charge-sheeted under Sections 17 and 40 UAPA; two receiving accounts attached.
lessons: A terror-funding node looks nothing like an operational cell: money and contacts carry the case while media and location are legitimately empty.
Do not treat an empty gallery in a UAPA case as a collection failure — record it, so the next fund-collection plan does not spend an hour on it.
Bank SMS is the durable copy of a payment history the accused has already cleared inside the application.

title: Factory-reset handset: almost every artifact was inaccessible, not empty
description: RC 15/2025 u/s 18 and 20 UAPA. Accused Kamran performed a full factory reset roughly ninety minutes before the search party reached the premises. The handset was seized already reset and had been signed back into its original account.

artifacts.note: The account re-added after the reset carried the device's prior identity and linked a second handset registered to the same account.
The restored-application list reproduced the pre-reset inventory, including two secure messengers the accused denied ever installing.
Restored from the account backup; two numbers matched the cell.
Synced history was restored to the device and was read in full. It contained nothing of interest — a genuine null, unlike the wiped stores.
Restored from the account and empty.
Factory reset; no database present on the device to read.
Factory reset; no application data present.
Message store destroyed by the reset; nothing existed to be read.
Call log destroyed by the reset.
Internal storage was re-provisioned at reset; no prior media remained on the device.

File-based encryption is re-keyed at factory reset, so the prior data is cryptographically unrecoverable. Six hours of carving returned nothing because nothing was readable, not because nothing was there.

outcome: Charge-sheeted on the account, application-inventory and second-handset evidence; co-accused declared an absconder.
lessons: A factory reset makes on-device artifacts inaccessible, not empty — grade every one of them 'inaccessible' so the tool keeps recommending them on the next handset that has not been reset.
Account-restored data (contacts, browser, calendar, application list) survives a reset and is often the only readable surface left.
Encryption re-keying at reset defeats carving; do not spend hours on deleted-record recovery on a handset that has been reset.

title: Ransom collected over UPI while the carrier call log stayed empty
description: FIR 176/2024 u/s 140(2) BNS, PS Motihari. Victim Bhavesh was abducted from outside his shop. Complainant Ramnath, his brother, received the demands. The handset examined was the complainant's, seized with consent within four hours.

artifacts.note: The ransom was collected in fourteen UPI transfers to six mule VPAs; the beneficiary device fingerprint resolved to a single handset.
Debit alerts preserved every VPA after the complainant's payment application history was cleared under instruction from the abductors.
The demand thread and two voice notes were still present; the audio was recovered from the shared-storage media folder without root.
A proof-of-life photograph received on WhatsApp. Its EXIF had been stripped by the application, but the room interior was matched to the confinement premises after the recovery.
The demanding number resolved to a SIM issued on a forged identity, which still narrowed the point of sale to one retailer.
Read in full. Every demand came as a WhatsApp voice call, so the carrier call log held no abductor contact at all.
The complainant's own movement history was read and was irrelevant — he never left his premises.
Read in full; nothing relevant.
Carving added nothing beyond the live thread.

outcome: Victim recovered on day three; four arrests; Rs 9 lakh of the ransom traced and frozen.
lessons: When the examined handset is the complainant's, the demand thread and the received media are the case — the abductor's carrier call log does not exist.
IP voice calls leave nothing in the call log; an empty log in a ransom case is a routing fact, not a collection failure.
Messaging applications strip EXIF from received images, so the evidential value of a proof-of-life photograph is its visible content, not its metadata.

title: Abduction complaint reframed by the subject's own social-app thread
description: FIR 92/2024 u/s 137(2) BNS, PS Jaunpur. Complainant Devendra alleged that accused Farhan had abducted his daughter Kiran, aged twenty-one. Kiran's own handset had been left at the residence and was examined.

artifacts.note: A nine-week direct-message thread recovered from direct.db on the rooted handset set out a planned departure and the meeting point.
A bus-ticket booking made from this handset two days before the alleged abduction, in the subject's own name.
Further thread fragments the subject had deleted were carved from the application cache.
Outgoing calls to the same number over six weeks.

Bank SMS and payment applications read in full: no ransom demand and no transfers of any kind. A real null that changed the working theory.
Read in full; operator messages only.
Nothing of evidentiary value in the gallery.

outcome: Subject traced and her statement recorded under Section 183 BNSS; abduction not made out and the FIR was closed as a mistake of fact.
lessons: An abduction complaint and a voluntary departure look identical at intake; the social-app thread on the subject's own handset is what distinguishes them.
Grade an absent ransom trail as a real 'none' — it is a finding that changes the offence, not a gap in collection.
A handset left behind by the subject is the most informative device in the case, not a discarded one.

title: Ephemeral-messaging offence proved on metadata and app-usage timing, not content
description: FIR 33/2024 u/s 8 POCSO Act and 75 BNS, PS Vashi. Accused Rohan was alleged to have sent sexual content to the victim, a fifteen-year-old, exclusively over an ephemeral messaging application over ten weeks. The handset was rooted at the laboratory.

artifacts.note: Root-recovered Arroyo database retained 412 conversation records with the victim's account across ten weeks. Content had auto-expired, but the send/receive pattern corroborated the victim's statement date by date.
Foreground usage statistics placed the application in use at each of the times the victim described, on each of the dates she named.
Handset placed at the address in the victim's statement on two of those dates.
Thumbnails of two saved snaps recovered from the application media cache.
Full gallery pull ran sixty-five minutes and produced nothing. The accused never saved to the camera roll, which is the expected pattern for this application.
direct.db read successfully; the accounts were connected but there were no direct messages between the parties.
Neither party was saved in the other's address book; contact was purely in-application.
Read in full; no calls between the parties.
Not installed on the handset.

outcome: Charge-sheeted under POCSO on the metadata and usage corroboration.
lessons: Ephemeral-messaging cases survive on metadata and app-usage timing, not content — an absence of saved media is the expected pattern and must be recorded as a 'none' rather than chased.
App-usage statistics can corroborate a victim's account of when contact occurred when no message body exists at all.
Root the handset for the Arroyo store even when you expect the content to be expired: the conversation record survives the content.

title: Image-circulation offence where the browser proved distribution, not just possession
description: FIR 118/2024 u/s 77 and 79 BNS r/w 67A IT Act, PS Ludhiana. Accused Gurpreet was alleged to have circulated intimate images of the victim Simran without consent after their relationship ended. The handset was rooted under warrant.

artifacts.note: The images were present in three directories, one of them the WhatsApp Sent media folder — establishing onward circulation, not mere possession.
Uploads to two image-hosting sites, with the resulting share URLs in history and the upload confirmations in cache.
Root-recovered cache4.db showed the same URLs posted to two public channels with a combined membership of eleven thousand.
Exported chat text showed the URLs shared into a group of forty-three.
Group membership resolved to twenty-nine identifiable recipients.
Six further images recovered from .trashed-.
direct.db read in full; the accused held an account but no relevant content or contact was on it.
No monetisation; payment artifacts read and empty.
Movement history read in full and irrelevant to an online-circulation offence.
Not installed.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; takedown orders issued to both hosts and the two channels.
lessons: In image-circulation offences the browser is where distribution is proven — possession is only half the offence.
The WhatsApp Sent media folder distinguishes a recipient from a distributor and is readable in shared storage without root.
Location is a genuine null in online sexual offences; recording it stops the next plan promising a movement narrative that will not exist.

title: Allegation where a uniformly empty artifact set was itself the finding
description: FIR 88/2024 u/s 74 BNS, PS Ambernath. Complainant Rekha alleged that accused Sandeep assaulted her at a warehouse between 19:00 and 20:30 on 4 March. The accused's handset was seized and examined the following day.

artifacts.note: Continuous GPS and Wi-Fi association placed the handset 38 km from the warehouse for the whole of the alleged window, with no gap.
Uninterrupted foreground activity across the same window, so the handset was in use and not merely left at that address.
A 22-minute call originating from that location inside the window, later confirmed by the other party.
Root-recovered database read in full; no contact of any kind between the parties, at any time.
direct.db read in full; no contact between the parties.
Neither party appeared in the other's address book.
Full gallery reviewed; nothing relevant.
Carving across all stores recovered nothing relevant.
Not installed.

outcome: Closure report filed after the location and usage findings were independently corroborated by the call recipient; no other material placed the accused at the premises.
lessons: An artifact set that is uniformly empty is a finding in its own right — record the negatives, because a case is resolved on them as often as it is charged on them.
Location and usage together answer a presence question that neither answers alone: one shows where the handset was, the other shows it was being carried.

title: SMS-forwarding trojan that wrote its own evidence into the outbound message log
description: FIR 402/2024 u/s 66C and 66D IT Act r/w 319(2) BNS, PS Cyber Crime Jaipur. Complainant Mahesh received a WhatsApp message with an APK styled as a bank utility. Three debits followed over eleven days. His handset was examined.

artifacts.note: A sideloaded package impersonating a bank utility, with SMS-read, SMS-receive and notification-listener permissions all granted at install.
The trojan forwarded every incoming message; the forwarding target number was itself recorded in the outbound SMS log, giving the first live lead.
The package had been removed remotely after the last debit; the package record and its install-source attribution were recovered.
The download link that delivered the APK, with the redirect chain intact.
The delivering message, from an unsaved number, preserved in an exported chat file.
Three beneficiary accounts from the debit alerts.
No unauthorised account was added; scope confirmed.
Read in full. There was never any voice contact — the whole compromise was silent.
Read and irrelevant to the offence.
Nothing relevant in the gallery.
Not installed.

outcome: Forwarding number and two mule accounts identified; one arrest in a neighbouring state; Rs 1.9 lakh recovered.
lessons: An SMS-forwarding trojan writes its own evidence into the outbound SMS log — the forwarding target is the first and fastest lead.
Recover the removed package record: uninstalling the malware does not remove its install-source attribution.
A silent compromise means the call log is genuinely empty; do not weight it in malware cases.

title: Task-fraud call centre run entirely inside one messaging workspace
description: FIR 517/2024 u/s 318(4) and 111 BNS r/w 66D IT Act, PS Cyber Crime Hyderabad. Accused Naman was picked up in a raid on a commercial premises operating a task-based investment fraud. Victims were recruited and handled without any telephone contact.

artifacts.note: Root-recovered cache4.db held the victim-handling group, the verbatim script, and the recruiter's daily assignment of targets to operators.
Commission credits into three accounts, reconciling exactly with the victim payment screenshots.
Four messaging accounts on one handset, all on virtual numbers.
A virtual-number application and a second-space cloner.
Screenshots of victim payment confirmations, used to claim commission.
Handset confined to a single commercial premises, identifying the call centre and eleven co-workers' devices at the same address.
Operator roster saved under first names.
Read in full and empty of anything relevant — the entire operation ran inside the messaging application, including the fake trading interface.
Read in full. Virtual numbers meant there was no carrier OTP traffic whatsoever.
Read in full and empty; no victim was ever telephoned.

outcome: Twelve arrests; premises sealed; forty-one linked victim complaints consolidated.
lessons: When an operation is run entirely inside one messaging application, browser, SMS and call logs are genuinely empty — record that, so the next task-fraud plan does not chase them.
Multiple application accounts on virtual numbers on one handset is itself the syndicate signature.
Location on a syndicate handset identifies the premises and therefore every other operator's device, which no chat thread does.

title: Anonymous defamation account attributed through accounts, cloner and usage timing
description: FIR 271/2024 u/s 79 and 356 BNS, PS Kalyani Nagar. Complainant Tanvi reported eleven defamatory posts from an anonymous handle. Suspect Yogesh was identified from a subscriber trail and his handset was seized. He had never contacted her directly.

artifacts.note: The anonymous handle was signed in on the handset alongside the suspect's own, sharing one recovery address.
The account-creation flow, the recovery-email confirmation and the handle-availability check, all timestamped.
The social application was in the foreground within ninety seconds of each of the eleven offending posts.
A dual-space cloner used to keep both profiles signed in at once.
The offending posts were still present in the application's local cache.
The doctored images in pre-post form, with the editing application's working files alongside them.
Two withdrawn posts recovered from cache.
Read in full. There was no contact between the parties at any time — which is the point of an anonymous account.
Read in full; no contact between the parties.
Root-recovered database read in full; the suspect never messaged the complainant directly.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; account preserved and disclosed under a Section 94 BNSS notice.
lessons: Anonymous-account harassment is an attribution problem, not a message-retrieval problem — accounts, app cloners and foreground-usage timing carry it.
The absence of any direct contact between the parties is consistent with, not contrary to, an anonymous-harassment allegation.
Pre-post working files of a doctored image are stronger attribution than the published image itself.

title: Group abuse where the complainant's own screenshots were the only surviving record
description: FIR 154/2024 u/s 79 and 351(2) BNS r/w the SC/ST Act, PS Sangli. Complainant Kailas reported sustained caste-based abuse in a workplace WhatsApp group. He had exited and cleared the group before filing. His own handset was examined.

artifacts.note: Sixty-one screenshots and two screen recordings of the group thread, all with intact file creation times spanning the period alleged.
The group participants had been saved with full names, identifying all nine senders shown in the screenshots.
The messaging application was in the foreground at every screenshot timestamp, consistent with contemporaneous capture rather than later assembly.
Fourteen further screenshots recovered from the .trashed- directory.
The complainant had exited and cleared the group; msgstore held no trace and the handset was unrooted, so the thread itself was never read.
Read in full; nothing relevant.
Read in full; nothing relevant.
Movement history read and irrelevant — the abuse was entirely online.
Empty.
Not applicable; payment artifacts read and empty.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; the screenshots were admitted with a Section 63 BSA certificate and the usage timeline as corroboration.
lessons: A complainant's own contemporaneous screenshots can be the whole case when the thread itself is gone — corroborate them with file creation times and foreground usage rather than dismissing them as secondary.
Clearing a chat on an unrooted handset makes the thread inaccessible, not empty; saying 'none' would teach the tool to stop asking for chat databases.
Ask the complainant for their handset early: victims routinely preserve what the accused has already destroyed.

title: Burglary solved on resale photographs when location history was switched off
description: FIR 203/2024 u/s 305 and 331(4) BNS, PS Sonipat. Accused Pankaj was suspected of a house burglary in which gold ornaments were taken. He kept location services disabled and there was no CCTV coverage on the approach.

artifacts.note: Photographs of the stolen ornaments laid out on a bedsheet, taken forty minutes after the burglary window and geotagged to the accused's rented room by the camera's own EXIF.
The same photographs in the Sent media folder, addressed to a jeweller, recovered from shared storage without root.
That recipient resolved to a jeweller subsequently arrested as a receiver.
One call to the jeweller four minutes before the images were sent.
Nine further images recovered from .trashed-.
Movement history was read in full and was empty for the entire period — the accused kept location services disabled. Read successfully; genuinely nothing there.
Read in full; operator messages only.
Read in full; nothing relevant.
Payment applications and bank SMS read; the sale was in cash and left no digital trace.
Installed; handset unrooted, cache4.db unreadable.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; ornaments recovered from the receiver under a Section 106 BNSS recovery memo.
lessons: Property crime is a disposal problem: the resale photograph and the receiver's contact matter more than the theft site itself.
An empty location history because the user disabled the service is a genuine 'none' — the artifact was read and simply held nothing, unlike a locked store.
Camera-app EXIF survives where a messaging application would have stripped it; always compare the gallery original against the sent copy.

title: Snatched handset attributed by what the new possessor added, not what the owner lost
description: FIR 341/2024 u/s 304(2) BNS, PS Andheri. Complainant Priyanka had her handset snatched at a signal. The device was recovered eighteen days later during an unrelated check and was examined as the stolen property itself.

artifacts.note: The complainant's account was removed and a new one added three hours after the snatching, identifying the possessor by name and recovery number.
Thirty-one applications installed in a single evening burst, establishing a change of user at a precise time.
Photographs taken with the device after the offence showed the possessor and the interior of his premises.
Post-offence movement identified a resale route through two intermediaries before the device settled at one address.
Outgoing calls after the offence resolved to the possessor's family.
The address book had been replaced wholesale from the new account's backup.
Carving ran for an hour. The complainant's own deleted data was never in issue and nothing relevant was recovered.
Read in full; nothing relevant.
Read in full; nothing relevant to the offence.
Re-registered by the new user, which removed the prior data; the new user's own database was crypt15 on an unrooted handset and unreadable.

outcome: Charge-sheeted against the possessor; two intermediaries identified from the movement trail.
lessons: On a recovered stolen handset the evidence is what the new possessor added, not what the owner lost — accounts, install bursts and post-offence media identify him.
An account change plus a same-evening install burst is a reliable change-of-user signature and dates the transfer of possession.
Do not run deep carving on a recovered handset by reflex: the owner's deleted data is rarely the question being asked.

title: Shop burglary where the planning was visible in search history before it was visible in movement
description: FIR 88/2025 u/s 305(a) and 331(3) BNS, PS Guwahati Paltan Bazar. Accused Bikash and co-accused Deepen were suspected of breaking into an electronics shop. They planned face to face and exchanged almost no messages.

artifacts.note: Searches for the shop's shutter-lock model, for an angle grinder, and eleven street-view lookups of the complainant's premises across the preceding fortnight.
Three passes of the premises at closing time on separate evenings before the night of the offence.
The browsing session the accused cleared the following morning was recovered from the browser's own history database freelist.
Co-accused contact immediately before and after each of the three passes.

outcome: Charge-sheeted; the angle grinder recovered at the co-accused's premises on the search-history lead.
lessons: Reconnaissance for property crime shows up as map lookups and product searches before it shows up as movement — browser is not a low-priority artifact in theft.
Co-accused who plan face to face leave a genuinely empty chat thread, while the call log still records the meetings being arranged.
Cleared browser history is recoverable from the history database's own free pages long after the user believes it is gone.

title: Missing adult traced along a UPI trail when location history was empty
description: Missing Person Report 27/2024, PS Muzaffarpur. Suraj, a thirty-four-year-old construction worker, left his room and stopped answering calls. Complainant Ramkishore, his employer, reported him untraceable after nine days. Suraj's spare handset, left in the room, was examined with family consent.

artifacts.note: UPI debit alerts from a bus operator, a dhaba and two roadside establishments reconstructed a 340 km route over three days.
Those alerts were the surviving copy: the payment application's own transaction history had been cleared, but the bank SMS remained.
A single outgoing call to a labour contractor in the destination district, four hours before the last payment.
That contractor was saved and traceable.
Location history was read in full and held nothing for the fortnight in question — the setting had been off for over a year. Read, and empty.
Read in full and empty; the handset was used only for calls and payments.

outcome: Located working at a site in the destination district on day eleven; no offence made out.
lessons: When location history is empty, payment alerts are the next-best movement record — a UPI trail is a route.
Bank SMS survives the clearing of the payment application's own history and is the artifact to reach for second.
Deep carving is the wrong tool in a live search; the fifty minutes it cost here bought nothing the live stores had not already given.

title: Missing student located through a second account the family did not know existed
description: Missing Person Report 09/2025, PS Kanpur Kakadeo. Anjali, aged eighteen, did not return from college. Complainant Harish, her father, reported her missing the same evening. She had deliberately left her handset at the residence and it was examined with his consent.

artifacts.note: A second mail account on the handset, unknown to the family, was the recovery address for a pseudonymous social profile.
That profile's direct messages set out the travel arrangement and named the person she was meeting, with the meeting point and time.
A hidden-vault application concealing the second profile's icon behind a calculator front end.

Train timetable lookups for the destination.

outcome: Located safe at the destination on day two; statement recorded and no offence made out.
lessons: A handset left behind is not a dead end — it holds the accounts and the application inventory that lead to where the person went.
Look for a second account and an app vault before concluding the social applications hold nothing; the profile that matters is usually not the one the family knows about.
An abandoned handset makes location a real 'none' — the record was complete and simply stopped, which is itself the signal that the departure was planned.

title: Low-usage handset where the last outgoing call was worth more than every other artifact
description: Missing Person Report 41/2024, PS Tirunelveli Town. Complainant Meenakshi reported that her father Shanmugam, aged seventy-three and diagnosed with early dementia, left the house at dawn and did not return. His handset was a basic smartphone he used almost exclusively for calls.

artifacts.note: The last outgoing call, at 06:40, was to a temple trust in a neighbouring district and gave the search its direction within twenty minutes of seizure.
That number was saved and resolved immediately, without a subscriber request.
A sparse eleven-application inventory told the team at once not to spend any effort on Tier-2 chat pulls.
One coarse network fix consistent with that direction; there was no GPS history because the setting had never been enabled.
Read in full; operator promotional messages only.
Read in full; the browser had never been opened.
Four photographs, all of family.
Empty.
No payment application installed and no bank SMS; read and empty.

Not installed.

outcome: Located at the temple the same evening, disoriented but unharmed.
lessons: A low-usage handset yields a very short evidence list, and that is the finding — read the installed-application inventory first and stop the expensive pulls early.
In an elderly or low-literacy missing-person case the last outgoing call is worth more than every other artifact combined.
An application that was never installed is 'inaccessible', not 'none': there was nothing to look at, so it says nothing about the artifact's value.
